plain: Should the federal government keep broad tariffs, which are taxes on goods imported into the United States? The rules changed several times in 2025 and 2026.

short_version.text: Tariffs are taxes paid by importers, and most of the cost has landed on U.S. buyers, about $1,100 a household a year by one estimate. Factory jobs fell rather than rose from April 2025 to February 2026, and courts struck down part of the tariffs. Supporters say they pressure trading partners and raise revenue.

connection.text: Tariffs come from the president acting under laws Congress passed, and the Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that one of those laws did not allow them. Congress can change those laws, so this bears most on your U.S. Senate and House races.

agree_means: Supports keeping the broad import taxes the president has imposed since 2025, accepting higher prices on some goods in return for trade leverage, revenue and support for U.S. industry.
disagree_means: Opposes broad tariffs and wants them ended or narrowed, accepting less trade leverage and less federal revenue in return for lower prices and less trade uncertainty.

research_notes: Claude in Chrome was not connected, so the bot-protected CBO tariff page (cbo.gov/publication/62704) was read in the built-in Browser pane; its source carries via: browser. Everything else was fetched directly. Double-check: (1) The Yale Budget Lab URL slug says april-8-2026 but the page is a living page now showing the Aug 24, 2026 update; its quotes may change when Yale updates it. (2) The USTR pages and the Skadden alert show no machine-readable date, so they use date_basis accessed. The CRS fact sheet is read through the everycrsreport.com mirror. (3) The Colorado governor's office pages are press releases from Gov. Polis (a Democrat) about state-agency reports; only the data sentences are quoted, and the $805 million figure is a conditional warning about escalation. The same report's claim that Colorado's effective tariff rate hit 21% was left out because it differs sharply from CBO's national estimate (15% peak) and the method was not checked. (4) The farmer quotes come from a forum hosted by Sen. John Hickenlooper (D). The Colorado Sun trade figures cover only the first five months of 2025; the full-year 2025 total comes from USTR. (5) Price-effect estimates differ by study (Yale 0.7% price level; PIIE cites studies from complete to incomplete pass-through). PIIE is a think tank that generally favors free trade. (6) A strong pro-tariff think-tank source was not obtained (American Compass was read in the browser but was a Feb 2025 excerpt, not used), so the case for tariffs rests on USTR and presidential statements and on revenue. (7) Not found: Colorado manufacturing job data, Colorado-specific refund amounts, or the Federal Circuit outcome on the Section 122 ruling.
